reference.topic: The auth service: the provider owns the conversation

claims.text: **product policy** — which identifier may register with which factor, whether open signup is allowed at all (read from the frozen auth-config via the pure resolvers, never re-implemented);
**the app's user row**, plus the consent and profile records the provider has no concept of;
**uniform errors**, so nothing leaks (see "No existence leaks" below).

Because the provider holds the flow state, the client can't re-negotiate what the config granted: it can only submit against a flow the server started, and every policy check runs again server-side on the submit.

reference.statement: The module keeps **no flow records**. A credential conversation is the provider's own flow, and the client holds its id. `AuthService` adds only what the provider cannot know:

claims.text: **The verify request is the atomic carrier.** Code, name, consents, and password travel together, so there is no moment where an account exists with its answers still in transit — either the whole thing lands, or nothing exists. A password identifier's password is a settings write at birth, never the registration credential; a config that collects one demands it at BOTH steps, so a hand-crafted verify can't slip past it.

**The DSL is the ONE authority on password acceptability.** The provider's own judgment calls are pinned off in its config (kratos.yml), the config validator keeps every DSL policy at or above the provider's hard floor (minLength ≥ 8; the shared check mirrors bcrypt's 72-byte max), and the form validates live with the SAME shared function the auth service enforces pre-birth (`shared/auth-config/password-policy`). A password the form accepted is a password the birth accepts.

After birth, failures degrade instead of stranding: a failed password WRITE (infrastructure, not policy) leaves a verified, passwordless account — code login and recovery both still work, and recovery sets a password; a failed consent or profile write is collected by the gate at `/resolve`. The account the provider accepted always stands. One failsafe guards the day a provider upgrade grows a password check the DSL doesn't know: a provider POLICY refusal at birth unbirths the seconds-old identity and answers a plain 400, so the retry is a clean redo — never a silent passwordless 201.

reference.statement: Every registration is a code registration: the code IS the credential proof, so the identity is born the moment it is proven — address verified from birth — and before that moment nothing exists anywhere but the provider's expiring flow record.

snippets.code:
GET  /auth/config?intent=registration&identifier=email
     → identifiers, factors, profileFields, consent   (what the screen must ask)

POST /auth/registration   { identifierType, identifierValue,
                            name?, consents?, password? }
     → the policy gauntlet runs (fast feedback for the form: identifier
       allowed, signup allowed, required profile, password policy), then the
       code is delivered. NOTHING exists yet — the password included: it
       stays with the client and rides the verify request
     → 202 { codeSent: true, flowId }

POST /auth/registration/verify   { flowId, identifier, code,
                                   name?, consents?, password? }
     → the gauntlet re-runs, authoritatively, while nothing exists yet
     → proves the delivered code — THE identity is born, address verified
       (the code was the proof), password SET on the fresh session when the
       config collects one, name + consent recorded
     → 201 { user }, signed in

reference.topic: Registration — one screen, one birth › Invitations
reference.statement: Accepting is always a **signed-in** action. A newcomer invited to an org registers plainly, returns via their intention, and accepts while signed in — the accept seats the membership, re-checks match strictness, records org-typed consent, and auto-verifies the invited address (possession was proven by delivery). See organizations.md (`./organizations.md`).

claims.text: **Password**: one call. Factor availability comes from the config; ANY failure (wrong password, unknown identifier, provider error) maps to one uniform 401. An identity provisioned outside a flow (a seeded admin) gets its app user row on first login (self-heal).
**Code (OTP)**: `start` ALWAYS answers with a flow id — see the masking note.

reference.topic: Login › 2FA — the gate's demand, not login's

claims.text: (`/me` is gate-excluded, so the step-up surface stays reachable while gated.) Consequence to know: TOTP protects exactly what the gate protects. An enrolled user with no gate-demanding membership gets no login-time enforcement from it — enrolment alone changes nothing about how they sign in.

reference.statement: Login has no second step. Every credential proof signs the caller in at whatever AAL it earned; a config that wants a TOTP-verified session says so with a membership-keyed `totp` rule, and THE GATE blocks the AAL1 session with `428 factor_session_verified(totp)` until the caller raises it on their live session:

snippets.code: POST /me/security/step-up  { code, method: totp | backup_code }  → AAL2

claims.text: UNIFORM for every account: nothing about the account's credentials is disclosed (the response never reveals whether a password already existed), and the finish always sets or rotates one.

Channel: the provider's recovery flow is email-only (its form validates email format), so **sms recovery rides the code-login proof** — the same delivered secret, equally fresh authentication for the privileged session.

snippets.code:
POST /auth/recovery/start     { identifier }               → { flowId }   (masked)
POST /auth/recovery/complete  { flowId, identifier, code } → signed in (cookie)
POST /auth/recovery/finish    { newPassword }                (a signed-in action)

reference.statement: Proving the code is a credential proof, so it signs the caller in like any other. `finish` acts on that session: it sets the new password (DSL policy first) and **revokes every session — the calling one included**, so only a fresh login works afterwards. The privileged window ends there.

claims.text: `loginCodeStart` and `recoveryStart` **always** answer with a flow id — the real one when the provider started a flow, an indistinguishable **decoy** when it refused. A decoy simply fails at submit, exactly like a wrong code.
Password login is already uniform provider-side (wrong password and unknown account return the same message); the auth service maps every failure to one 401 regardless.

reference.statement: Kratos's code-login start REFUSES an unknown identifier with a distinct error (message `4000035`, "This account does not exist…"), which would make accounts enumerable by anyone who can POST. The auth service therefore never passes that through:
`/me/security/*` — the caller's own 2FA controls. Every one acts on the session token from the caller's OWN cookie (never a request-supplied id), and that token never appears in a response:

snippets.code:
GET  /me/security              { totpEnrolled, backupCodesGenerated }
POST /me/security/totp/enroll  → { flowId, totpSecret, qrDataUrl }
POST /me/security/totp/confirm { flowId, code } → { backupCodes }  (shown once)
POST /me/security/backup-codes → { backupCodes }  (regenerate)
POST /me/security/step-up      { code, method }   raise the session to AAL2
POST /me/security/totp/disable requires a prior step-up (provider demands AAL2)
POST /me/security/sessions/revoke-others   sign out every other device. Native
                               to the provider: with no session table of our own
                               there is no second store that could disagree about
                               which sessions are live. The caller's survives.

reference.topic: The gate: live evaluation, facts not verdicts

claims.text: Resolve obligations from the **current** config for two families of context (see Two families of context below):
— **membership** — `{membershipOrgType}` + one per held role. Everything a matching rule demands stands, session facts included.
— **registration invariants** — `{intent: "registration"}`, plus one context per identifier type the caller **owns**. Persistent requirements only.
Check each obligation against **live facts**:
— `identifier_verified` → provider's verifiable addresses
— `factor_session_verified` → this session's proven methods / AAL
— `profile_data_provided` → profile row (fixed columns, then `data[field]`)
— `legal_consent_granted` → consent record at the CURRENT published version (unpublished document = waived + warning, never bricks the app)

Unmet obligations → `428 { obligations }`; the client routes blocked callers to `/resolve` through two layers. On NAVIGATION, the app's route guard — attached to the whole signed-in shell, so every signed-in page is gated by default — probes `gate/check` and redirects to `/resolve` with the blocked page as `?intention=`. On any IN-PAGE request that lands 428, the module's client fires its gate-blocked hook and the provider does the same redirect — seeding the gate query so `/resolve` paints instantly, latching so a burst of parallel 428s navigates once, and skipping only `/resolve` itself so a caller mid-resolution is never yanked away. `?intention=` carries only in-app paths; `/resolve`'s Continue button takes the caller back. EVERY obligation resolves ON `/resolve`: the page is a wizard that mounts one resolver at a time, in the gate's order — LEGAL CONSENT FIRST, from every scope (ReconsentCard — see legal.md (`./legal.md`), fed by `GET /legal/consent/pending`): a caller agrees to the terms before anything else is asked of them. Then the rest in the order the gate collected them — identifiers (IdentifierResolution), TOTP (TwoFactorCard), profile fields (ProfileDataForm). The page exemptions that used to shadow the server's excludePaths (`/account/profile`, `/account/security`) are gone; the ENDPOINT excludes (`/me`, `/legal/`) remain — resolution must stay callable while blocked.
Consequences, by design:
Add an obligation to the config (or publish a new T&C version) and every existing user who doesn't meet it is blocked on their **next request** — no migration, no stale "gate passed" flag.

The db stores facts (consents, profile fields), the provider stores facts (verified addresses, session methods); requirements live only in config. Facts can't go stale; requirements are always current.
The only cache anywhere is a ~30s whoami facts cache. Never cache a verdict.

Membership facts are **live** and ride on the **session**: the session middleware resolves the caller's org-context once (`SessionService.resolve` via `MembershipService.listMemberships`) — active org + membership roles — and the gate reads the roles off `c.get("session").memberships` rather than re-fetching.

reference.statement: The gate stores **no verdict**. Per request:

claims.text: **Membership contexts** are unfiltered. Belonging to an org is what makes its demands legitimate, so _everything_ a matching rule asks for stands — session facts included (an org type may demand a password-verified session, or a TOTP step-up for a role). An obligation the caller cannot satisfy yet — a verified email they don't have — is a real instruction: go add one.

The identifiers MAP joins this lens as an invariant: every membership context keeps at least one identifier type it accepts. The map carries no `require` of its own, so the gate derives it — a caller who owns _only_ types a context excludes gets an `identifier_present` obligation listing the types that context accepts (any one satisfies it). Holding an excluded type is fine; holding nothing else is not. This is also why removing an identifier is never refused for config reasons: the mutation stays permissive, and the gate walks the caller back through `/resolve` — the same answer it gives a phone-only user who _joins_ such an org by invitation.

**Registration invariants** answer a question flows can't. Registration is where the product states what an account must carry (a verified address, a name, platform consent), but a flow only enforces its rules _while it runs_. Birth-at-verify means the registering address can't leave unverified anymore — what the invariants still guard is everything else that can drift afterwards: an identifier ADDED post-birth whose verification was abandoned, a consent or profile write that failed at birth, an account seeded outside the flow. So the gate re-checks what registration establishes, evaluating `{intent: "registration"}` for every signed-in caller. Two filters keep that honest:

**Persistent requirements only.** `factor_session_verified` describes the moment credentials are proven, not a fact the account carries. Made standing it would pin every session to the method registration used — and a config that offers both password and code login (ours does) would gate its own login.

**Owned identifier types only.** "Registration requires a verified email" means _if this account has an email, it is verified_ — not _every account must grow one_. A phone-only account owes nothing about email. This is precisely why membership rules skip the filter: an org that genuinely demands an address the caller lacks says so with a membership-keyed rule.

Both families fold in the caller's org types, so a `notWhen` carve-out — the `system_admin` break-glass exemption from consent — keeps holding in either lens. Scoping differs, though: registration-invariant CONSENT is checked at the PLATFORM scope (where registration records it) for every signed-in caller, so a republished platform document re-gates members and org-less callers alike; org-typed documents are the membership lens's demand.

The DSL is untouched by this: no new keys, no rule migration. `intent: "registration"` + a persistent requirement simply _means_ "an account invariant", and the gate is its second reader (the registration flow being the first). Cost is one provider identity read per gated request, shared with the obligation checks below it.
Consequences, by design:
An account is born with its registering address verified, so no window exists in which a fresh unverified account roams a gated app. Anyone who abandons the code step simply has no account.

A seeded `system_admin` owner owes the config's admin standing obligations — verified email, a password-verified session, and TOTP. TOTP can't be seeded, so on first login the admin is `428`-blocked and lands in the `/resolve` wizard, which mounts the enrolment flow in place (its `/me/security/*` endpoints are under the gate's `/me` exclude prefix, so they answer while gated). This is correct behaviour, not a seed bug — the gate is doing its job.
Adding an identifier and abandoning _its_ verification gates you until you finish. Consistent with "verify what you own", and deliberate.

reference.statement: The gate reads the same config through two lenses, and the difference is the whole design.
